Climate adaptation However, there is limited evidence on whether these shelters are equitably accessible to those most at risk. This Climate shelters study addresses this gap by assessing the accessibility of shelters in Barcelona using a mobility justice framework. Mobility justice We ask: how do the spatial distribution of climate shelters and the socioeconomic characteristics of urban Social inclusion neighbourhoods jointly shape inequalities in access for vulnerable populations in Barcelona? We aim to (1) assess the spatial and temporal accessibility of shelters within a 10-min walk, using a reduced walking speed (3.28 km/ h); and (2) analyse the socioeconomic profiles of neighbourhoods with and without access. Using GIS-based isochrone analysis and socioeconomic data, we map access to shelter for adults aged 65+, while also exam- ining intersectional vulnerabilities, including income level and migrant background. Results show that while 92 % of vulnerable residents live within 10 min of a shelter, this drops to 75 % in August due to seasonal closures. Accessibility gaps are most pronounced in low-income and migrant-dense areas. We conclude that spatial proximity alone is not enough. Without addressing mobility limitations and social inequalities, climate adap- tation policies risk exacerbating existing disparities. Our findings aim to provide evidence-based recommenda- tions for achieving Barcelona’s 2030 goal of universal 5-min access, and a framework for equitable climate adaptation evaluation for other cities. 1. Results To address our research question - how do the spatial distribution of climate shelters and the socioeconomic characteristics of neighbour- hoods jointly shape inequalities in access for vulnerable populations in Barcelona? - we conducted a geospatial analysis, as outlined in the previous section. We began our analysis by mapping the distribution of vulnerable populations across the city, focusing on adults aged 65–79 and 80+(Fig. 4). These demographic data were then overlaid with the spatial distri- bution of climate shelters, and 10-min walking areas were calculated using an adjusted walking speed for older adults (Fig. 5). This analysis revealed areas with good access and those with significant deficits. Notably, areas with inadequate coverage tend to be concentrated in the Sants-Montjuïc and Les Corts districts in the south-west, near the border with L’Hospitalet de Llobregat, and in the Sant Andreu and Nou Barris districts in the north-east. These areas tend to be high-density with relatively few climate shelters. To quantify the access, we evaluated the number of vulnerable res- idents within the 10-min walk coverage area (Table 2). The results show that around 92 % of vulnerable residents in Barcelona - approximately 320,500 people - live within a 10-min walk of a climate shelter. This includes 212,900 adults aged 65–79 and 107,600 adults aged 80 and over. The remaining 28,650 vulnerable residents live more than 10 min away, comprising 18,690 people aged 65–79 and 9960 people aged 80+. Similar proportions in both age groups suggest that proximity-based access has been distributed equitably by age. JSON: Name: climate_shelter_mobility_access Title: GIS-based network isochrone analysis of climate shelters to quantify mobility-constrained accessibility inequalities for heat-vulnerable urban residents Short Hypothesis: Applying a reduced walking speed of 3.28 km/h for older adults and enforcing observed seasonal shelter closures reduces the share of heat-vulnerable residents within a 10-minute walk, and these reductions are proportionally larger in low-income and high foreign-born neighbourhoods than in high-income neighbourhoods. Related Work: Existing approaches estimate access to urban services using time-based proximity (x-minute city) implemented via Euclidean buffers or network isochrones with standard walking speeds. Variants include simple population-to-facility coverage rates at census-tract scale and more detailed network-based isochrones that incorporate pedestrian networks and slope. Mobility-justice and intersectional analyses have been proposed conceptually to expose socio-spatial inequities, and separate studies examine thermal exposure and cooling center usage patterns. Reported limitations across methods are: reliance on aggregate census units that mask intra-unit heterogeneity; use of a single, standard walking speed that overestimates access for mobility-constrained groups; Euclidean buffers that ignore network topology and elevation; omission of temporal facility availability (seasonal/weekly closures) and facility capacity/usage; and limited incorporation of intersectional socioeconomic variables into spatial accessibility metrics. No existing operational pipeline systematically combines network isochrones with mobility-adjusted speeds, temporal availability, fine-grained demographic grids, and quantitative disparity metrics for climate-shelter access. Abstract: This project quantifies mobility-constrained access inequalities to urban climate shelters by combining network-based isochrone modelling with mobility-adjusted walking speeds and temporal shelter availability. Focusing on Barcelona, we integrate a 100×100 m demographic grid of age, income, and foreign-born share with a pedestrian network and shelter database (locations, types, opening days). We generate shelter catchments using slope-adjusted network isochrones at a 3.28 km/h walking speed for adults 65+, compute population coverage within 10-minute and 5-minute thresholds, and compare results to baselines using standard walking speeds and Euclidean buffers. We calculate per-district and per-quantile disparity metrics and run ablations varying speed, availability, and spatial aggregation. The main contribution is an operational, reproducible pipeline that produces robust, quantitative measures of how mobility constraints and operational availability change proximity-based shelter coverage and which neighbourhoods are disproportionately impacted. Expected outcomes include precise estimates of coverage loss due to mobility and seasonal closures, ranked lists of underserved areas, and policy-ready equity metrics to guide shelter deployment and operations. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Barcelona Climate Shelter Network (geolocated shelters, facility type, opening days/calendar 2019–2024), (2) Única360 demographic grid 100×100 m (age groups including 65–79, 80+; household income per capita; foreign-born share), (3) pedestrian network and crossings from OpenStreetMap, (4) elevation raster/DTM for slope adjustments, (5) administrative district boundaries; optional: shelter capacity data if available. Baselines: B1: network isochrones with standard walking speed 5.0 km/h, full availability; B2: Euclidean buffers computed for 10-min distance equivalent to 5.0 km/h; B3: aggregated census-tract coverage using standard speed and full availability. Primary method: network isochrones with walking speed 3.28 km/h, slope-adjusted speed, and observed opening days. Evaluation metrics: overall coverage (%) of vulnerable population (65+ and 80+), coverage reduction (%) vs baselines, per-district coverage, coverage by income decile and foreign-born decile, disparity ratio (coverage_top_decile / coverage_bottom_decile), Gini coefficient over spatial units, mean and median walking time to nearest shelter, logistic regression odds ratio for being covered (predictors: income, foreign-born share, population density), spatial autocorrelation (Moran’s I) of coverage residuals, and bootstrap 95% CIs for coverage metrics. Experimental setup: 1) compute per-shelter network isochrones for 10-min and 5-min thresholds using the pedestrian network and slope-adjusted travel speeds (software: OSMnx/NetworkX or CARTO isoline API, PostGIS for spatial joins); 2) intersect isochrone polygons with 100×100 m demographic grid to sum covered population; 3) quantify metrics for primary method and baselines; 4) ablation studies: A1) walking-speed sensitivity {2.5, 3.28, 4.0, 5.0} km/h; A2) availability scenarios {full availability, observed opening days, worst-case August closures}; A3) spatial aggregation sensitivity {100 m grid vs census tracts}; A4) topology sensitivity {network isochrone vs Euclidean buffer}; 5) statistical tests: bootstrap (n=1,000) for metric CI, permutation test to compare district-level coverage differences, and logistic regression with cluster-robust SEs; 6) optional capacity simulation: assign per-shelter capacities from available metadata or synthetic distribution and compute percent of population within reachable shelters under capacity constraints. Outputs: per-scenario maps, per-district and per-quantile tables, disparity metric panels, significance test results, and ablation plots. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data quality and coverage biases: demographic grid may undercount undocumented migrants or recent movers; shelter dataset may omit informal cooling sites; opening-day records may be incomplete or change year-to-year. Mobility model limitations: single speed per age group ignores intra-group heterogeneity (health, disability, carrying loads); slope-adjusted speed models approximate but do not capture micro-topography or pedestrian infrastructure quality. Omitted variables: shelter capacity, thermal performance, perceived safety, and awareness/use are not represented; these omission limit interpretation from proximity to effective access. Temporal limitations: static residential population used instead of diurnal population flows; results may misrepresent daytime exposure. External validity: pipeline calibrated on Barcelona may not generalize to cities with different street networks, shelter typologies, or demographic patterns without recalibration. Computational scalability: high-resolution network isochrones for thousands of facilities and fine grid cells require substantial compute and memory; performance may degrade for larger metropolitan regions. Causal inference limits: spatial association between income/migrant share and coverage does not demonstrate causality; confounding by urban form and historical infrastructure allocation may persist.
